content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper proposes a representation learning method for a geospatial scene data (represented by points, polylines, and polygons). The main idea is to use the contrastive representation learning method such as SimCLR on this geospatial data. Because the input is not an image, the authors proposes a new augmentation method, similarity measure, padding, etc. The experiment is performed on spatial scene retrieval task and a classification task and show better performance that previous the baselines. 

Strength. The geospatial representation learning is an interesting challenge. The approach is reasonable. The empirical result is good.

Weakness. The most significant weakness is the overall clarity of the paper. The paper seems rushed and the updated version does not show much improvement in this sense. For example, Fig 1 seems the most important figure to understand the model but actually very hard to understand accurately. Technical novelty is also marginal to the audience of this general ML community because it is basically applying contrastive representation learning to different input modality. Some geospatial learning conference might be a better fit to submit this.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: Due to the weakness described above.

content.title: Initial response to zUDF
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for these comments and suggestions. Our response to these comments are provided below:

**#1 From the introduction neither a clear problem statement nor the contribution is apparent.**  
A1: Our main goal is to build a general representation model for spatial scene data and apply it into multiple downstream tasks. Moreover, our main contributions are stated at the end of our Introduction.

**#2 Figs.1 and 2 do not make much sense and do not help to understand the problem and its solution.**  
A2: Figs.1 implies three different situations of spatial scenes which often emerge in real-world data. And we have updated Figs.2 and their captions to make them more clear.

**#3 The technical discussion is Sec.4 is insufficient.**  
A3: We have add some detail imformations in appendix (See Table 7 and 8).

**#4 the mathematical writing must be seriously checked and the bibliography entries need to be checked.**  
A4: We have checked our mathematical writing and bibliography entries carefully and corrected error statements.

content.title: Initial response to WYQJ
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments and suggestions. Our response to these comments are provided below:

**#1 Will the spatial scence augmentation give unfair advantages to Scene2Vec?**  
A1: We are very sorry that the composition of the test data was wrongly stated in our paper. We have revised the statement. Our test data consists of two parts, 150 real raw spatial scene data and 350 spatial scene data generated from our augmentation method instead of only 500 spatial scene data generated from our augmentation method. It means that our test data can guarantee the fairness of the experiments results.

**#2 It is still not clear to me how point sets of polylines or polygons are properly augmented. In addition, what is the criteria of choosing point sets for these structures.**  
A2: We have added the table of algorithm of our augmentation method in the appendix (See Algorithm 1). Our criteria for augmenting the polyline and polygon data types is randomly sampling points on polylines or on the edges of polygons according to their geometry structures.

**#3  Some details seems missing such as the final lengths after padding after augmentation module, training and testing profile.**  
A3: We have added the parameter selection section in our appendix (See Sec A.2).

**#4 Lack of ablation of key design modules.**  
A4: We have added ablation study to investigate different components of our spatiual scene augmentation method (See Table 7). We also have added ablation another study to investigate how the number of padding points will affect the model performance (See Table 8).

content.title: Initial response to fGyE
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments and suggestions. We have grouped our answers into several topics with detailed explanations:

**#1: the technical novelty is marginal for machine learning.**  
A1: Our main novelties can be summarized as the following three points:  
1)There is very limited research on unsupervised learning for spatial scenes despite its importance in various geospatial applications.  So our work should be treated as the SOTA work on spatial scence encoding for all following research. We think bringing a novel geospatial task to the general AI domain is one critical contribution of our work.  
2)Due to the irregularity of spatial data types envolved in spatial scences, all previous works focus on encoding spatial scences by either first rasterizing them as images or only considering one spatial data types (e.g., points). However, the rasterization process can lead to significant information loss and how to decide the appropraite raster cell is difficult -- the well-known the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP). On the other hand, only treating geospatial entities as points will lead to singificant information simplification and many information spatial relations are loss.  As far as we know, we are the first work that jointly consider all geometry types (including points, polylines, and polygons) for spatial scence encoding.  
3)We proposal a novel spatial scence augmentation method which is specially designed for polygons and polygons by considering the unique structures of both geometry types. We show that this kind of augmentation method is very useful for generating good positive/negative pairs for contrastive learning. We expect this novel spatial scence augmentation method will be adopted as the default spatial scence augmentation methods for future research just like color jitter, translation, rotation for image augmentation.

**#2 The experiments cannot support its claim that it can support multiple geospatial tasks.**  
A2: Spatial scene similarity is the basic of spatial cognition which is the basic of multiple geospatial tasks. To show the effectiveness of our Scene2Vec model, we mainly conduct two spatial scene retrieve experiments to evaluate our model. Next, we also design two experiments (classification and clustering) to show the performance of our model for two additional tasks -- spatial data type classification (Table 5) and land use classification (Table 6)

**#3 Some relevant recent papers with similar idea have not been discussed in related work.**  
A3: Just as we mentioned in #1, there is very limited research on unsupervised learning for spatial scenes and most of them are proposed in the field of geographic information.Moreover, we have discussed most of these researches in our article (Section 1 and 2). Our work can be considered as a breakthrough on spatial scene task that combining geoinformatic theory and machine learning models.

content.title: Initial response to otAm
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments and suggestions. Our response to these comments are provided below:

**#1 Ablation study on the number of padding points:**  
A1: Padding operation is designed for augmenting the polyline and polygon data types by adding randomly sample points on polylines or on the edge of polygons according to their geometry structures.  We have added experiments with different padding points in the appendix (See table 8) to further show that our padding method is efficient and stable in our experiments. The overall result shows a trend of first rising and then falling, we consider the main reason is as the number of points increases, the complexity of the entire data increases geometrically, which will affect the experimental results to some extent.

**#2 Improving Figure 2 to show the role of contrastive learning.**  
A2: We have already updated our Figure 2 and add some concrete explanations to make it more clear to everyone. Moreover, figure 2(a) refers to overall workflow of our model while figure 2(b) refers to our Scene2Vec encoder architecture corresponding to 'encoder k' and 'encoder q' in figure 2(a). 

**#3 Page 4, last line: "where l is a hyper-parameter', it will read better if "l" is a math symbol "$l$". Currently, it looks like the number "1".**  
A3: Thanks for your advising, we have already corrected some errors in our article like you mentioned above.

**#4 Code.**  
A4: We will make our implementation public with the final version of our paper.

The proposed approach seems to outperform simple baselines for the tackled benchmarks.


Weaknesses:

content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
In general, the approach seems to be novel. However, due to the quality and clarity of the presentation this is not fully clear. Thus, the presentation must be seriously overworked, including the following points: 

From the introduction neither a clear problem statement nor the contribution is apparent.

Figs.1 and 2 do not make much sense and do not help to understand the problem and its solution.

The related work section is rather short and structured insufficiently. Some parts are already discussed in the introduction. Thus, it would be better to merge both sections to make the problem and the contribution more apparent.

The technical discussion is Sec.4 is insufficient. Even when reading the section multiple times the details are still unclear. Moreover, it stays unclear where just existing ideas are discussed and where new, own contributions are presented.

Moreover, the mathematical writing must be seriously checked!

The presented experimental results indicate an improvement to the baselines, however, it is not fully clear how these results could be interpreted correctly.

The bibliography entries need to be checked!

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a representation learning approach for geographic spatial map data leveraging contrastive learning. Inspired by Space2Vec and MoCo, this work encodes the relative distance and attributes (e.g., categories) of point sets within spatial scenes via MLPs and learns in a self-supervised manner with proposed scene augmentation strategy. Experiment on real-world spatial data show that higher performance of scene retrieval based on points only and complete geospatial data is achieved compared to baselines including KNN and space2vec.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

Though I am not very familar with topic of geospatial data, overall I think this paper tries to tackle an interesting problem of learning useful representations of geospatial data which are discriminative enough for downstream tasks including scene retrieval, classification. Experiments show the effectiveness of the method with a clear performance gain on the selected dataset.

Weaknesses

- In Sec5.2.1, testing data are generated using the data augmentation pipeline proposed in this work and this could give Scene2Vec unfair advantages in my opinion as the augmentation strategy is applied directly during training (I assume that results in Sec5.2.2 are also obtained in the same way. But please correct me if I am wrong). Though there is still insight from Table3, I am wondering if it is possible to evaluate on raw spatial data instead of augmented ones to better reflect the overall performance of Scene2Vec.

- It is still not clear to me how point sets of polylines or polygons are properly augmented. In addition, what is the criteria of choosing point sets for these structures.

- Some details seems missing such as the final lengths after padding after augmentation module, training and testing profile.

- Lack of ablation of key design modules.
Related to last point, though several tasks are evaluated, there lacks of necessary ablation and discussions about the key contributions such as the benefits of different components in augmentation.

- In definition 1, shoud $c_i$ be $c_j$?  $ d_j = [x_{j1} − c_i, ...] $ or  $ d_j = [x_{j1} − c_j, ...] $

- Writing quality needs to be improved.
There are several typos, missing spaces and incomplete sentences in the main text. For example, 
    - footnote of page3, a tree instead of A tree
    - beginning of sec 5.2.1, Considering that xxx, Since points are xxx
    - ...
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This submission show an interesting application by adpoting existing self-supervised preresentation learning techniques in the area of geospatial data with specifically designed encoding and augmentation strategy. The overall formulation of self-supervision is not novel (Space2Vec, MoCo, SimCLR), but there is some insight in transferring them to geospatial data.

The clarity and quality of writing is relatively low. More efforts in formatting, writing and details are required to fully understand the details.

There is currently no appendix and codes attached,  with the missing details (see weaknesses) section, I am not sure if it is possible to fully reproduce the results, A vanilla version should be dobale.
content.summary_of_the_review: This submisison could be helpful to the topic of processing geograpical data. However, there are unclear descriptions and missing details.Based on my own understanding of the paper and mentioned baselines, I lean to a borderline rejection but may adjust my rating based on other expert reviews within this specific topic and whether my concerns are properly addressed.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a general  spatial scene representation model called Scene2Vec for spatial scenes that contain different spatial data types including points, polylines and polygons. The model can be trained in an unsupervised manner related to contrastive loss. We conduct two experiments on spatial scenes retrieval tasks with spatial objects based 1) purely on points and 2) on three spatial data types. The analysis shows that Scene2Vec has the ability to encode various spatial data types and performs better than other baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1) The clamined major novelty is the general-purpose spatial scene encoder framework, Scene2Vec, which uses
multi-scale location encoding methods to model relative spatial relations among spatial objects in a spatial scene. The solution may be novel for the geographic application filed but not new for general machine learning. 
2) Contrastive learning which allows un-supervised learning is just an incremental technical contribution. 
3) The authors claim the method can handle multiple geospatial tasks but most of the experiments only focus on retrieval. 
4) Some relevant recent papers with similar idea have not been discussed in related work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The technical clarity  is good.  
Novelty is generally marginal.
It can be reporduced with some efforts.
The general quality is around the boardline of ICML.

I would like to recommend "marginally below the acceptance threshold" because the following points: 
1) the technical novelty is marginal for machine learning, 
2) the position of the technical novelty is not clear and some important references (not for geo-spatial scenes) are not discussed, 
3) the experiments cannot support its claim that it can support multiple geospatial tasks.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a multi-scale spatial scene encoding model, Scene2Vec, to encode spatial data of geographic objects into feature vectors. The learning is formulated in a contrastive learning scheme in which points, polylines, and polygons are unified in one framework. A novel spatial scene augmentation method has been proposed to generate contrastive pairs. Experiments on scene retrieval tasks show that the proposed method outperforms others by a margin.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
- The intuition of generating augmented multi-scale spatial scenes and learning robust representations from a contrastive learning setting makes sense to me. 

- The augmentation mechanism is quite interesting.

- The Scene2Vec workflow is well-designed. 

- The experiment results are solid.

### Weakness
I think the padding operation in Section 4.1 is interesting. But it is unclear to me how much of an impact it has on the final results. In Figure 2, it seems to me that the padded points (in gray) are of significant numbers compared to existing points in the scene. I wonder how does the number of padding points per scene would affect the quality of the features and/or the final scene retrieval performance. Maybe I have missed it but I couldn't find this information in the experiment section. This is my main concern.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity

The paper is straightforward and easy to follow. Some editing suggestions:
1. Figure 2 could use some improvement in design. Currently, it is not clear from the figure itself how would contrastive learning (a) fits into the overall workflow (b). Using consistent notations between the subfigures would be helpful. 
2. Page 4, last line: "where l is a hyper-parameter', it will read better if "l" is a math symbol "$l$". Currently, it looks like the number "1".

### Quality

The quality of the work is adequate. 

### Novelty

While multiple individual components are borrowed or heavily inspired from prior work (especially Mai et al. 2019), the main idea of augmenting spatial scenes + contrastive learning seems to be a novel combination. 

The contrastive learning section (Sec. 4.2) is pretty standard with configurations from prior established works. It might be more interesting if there is any modification on the contrastive loss that is spatial data-specific. Yet, the current setting is fine for the task.

### Reproducibility
There seems to be a sufficient amount of detail in the paper for reproducibility. It will be better if the authors plan to release their code. It is not currently mentioned in the submission.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper proposes a novel contrastive learning workflow that is powered by spatial scene augmentations. Experiments show that such a design outperforms other alternatives by a solid margin. There are concerns mentioned in the "Weakness" section above, but I believe the paper would be a valuable contribution to researchers that are interested in learning robust spatial representations.

content.title: Contrastive Representation Learning for Multi-scale Spatial Scenes
content.abstract: Spatial scenes, which are composed by spatial objects and their spatial relations, are the basis of geographic information retrieval, spatial cognition, and spatial search. Despite the wide usage of spatial scenes, representation learning on spatial scenes that contain complex composition of spatial objects remains a challenge, since the spatial data types of geographic objects (e.g., points, polylines, and polygons) and the geographical scales vary across different spatial scenes. Inspired by recently proposed multi-scale location encoding models such as Space2Vec, we propose a multi-scale spatial scene encoding model called Scene2Vec to solve these representational challenges. In Scene2Vec, a location encoder is used to model the spatial relationships among spatial objects and a feature encoder is used for objects' semantic feature encoding. A scene encoder is developed to integrate the representations of spatial objects into a single scene embedding. Moreover, we propose a spatial scene augmentation method to sample additional points based on the shapes of polyline/polygon-based spatial objects in all scales of spatial scenes. The whole model is trained in a self-supervised manner with a contrastive loss. We conduct experiments on real world datasets for spatial scene retrieval task 1) purely based on points, e.g., points of interest (POIs), and 2) based on multi-structured spatial objects. Results show that Scene2Vec outperforms well-established encoding methods such as Space2Vec and multi-layer perceptrons due to the advantages of the integrated multi-scale representations and the proposed spatial scene augmentation method. Moreover, detailed analysis shows that Scene2Vec has the ability to generate representations of all the three types of spatial objects in a multi-scale manner.
